hook: In nineteen eighty-three, the alarms said: missiles incoming.

captions.hook_line: In 1983, one man's gut feeling may have stopped a nuclear war ☢️
captions.body: On September 26, 1983, Soviet duty officer Stanislav Petrov saw the early-warning system report one, then five US missile launches. A real first strike would involve far more missiles and ground radar showed nothing, so he reported a false alarm. It was later traced to sunlight reflecting off high clouds.
captions.comment_prompt: Would you have trusted the system or your gut?

youtube_title: The Man Who Didn't Start a Nuclear War

blocks.narration: In nineteen eighty-three, the alarms said: missiles incoming. One Soviet officer had only minutes to decide what to do.

blocks.narration: His name was Stanislav Petrov, the duty officer at a warning center. The screens showed one launch, then five.

A round green radar screen on the Console with one bright blip, then five blips appearing

blocks.narration: His orders: report an attack up the chain. That could have triggered a nuclear counterstrike. But something felt off.

blocks.narration: A real first strike would mean hundreds of missiles, not five. Ground radar saw nothing. He called it a false alarm.

blocks.narration: He was right: the satellites had mistaken sunlight on high clouds for launches. Five missiles that were never there.
